On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape Udayaditya commands Sitaram to open the locked inner-quarters door, threatens to fight him, and, after Sitaram refuses to fight because Udayaditya twice saved his life, Udayaditya takes Sitaram's weapon and binds him head to foot at Sitaram's request so Sitaram will be spared punishment by the Maharaj. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison Sitaram opens the prison door, grabs Udayaditya and almost carries him out, and while the helpless Udayaditya asks what to do and where to go, Sitaram takes charge and leads him, saying, "Come, come with me!"

Pratapaditya initially ordered two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; one brother lured Basanta Ray's retainers away by claiming dacoits had attacked the village, but the other refused to carry out the killing. Later, after Muktiyar Khan delivered Pratapaditya's signed death order, Abdul killed Basanta Ray with a drawn sword in his room.
1. In the inner quarters/Mahishi's room, disguised as a middle-aged woman; 2. In the palace room with the king, as the jester Ramai Bhand
The Rajmahishi secretly sends Matangini to Mangala (Rukmini) to fetch poison, and Surma dies from poisoning before she can be exiled to her father's house.
Her husband Ramchandra Ray takes another wife and permanently rejects her, so when she finally reaches Chandradwip she finds him marrying someone else and he will not forgive her.

Udayaditya throws his signet ring to Rukmini when she demands it, and Rukmini brings the ring — which has a seal with the Yubaraj's name engraved on it — to Sitaram and Bhagavat. Sitaram and Bhagavat use that seal to stamp a forged petition falsely accusing Udayaditya of lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor in order to get the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat delivers the sealed petition to Pratapaditya, claiming it was being taken to Delhi by a servant of Udayaditya who has fled, and Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya imprisoned after reading it.

The midnight escape led to Sitaram and Bhagavat being dismissed as guards; Udayaditya then gave them monthly stipends, Pratapaditya forbade any further help, Surma continued the payments secretly through a maid who revealed them to Mangala, and when word of the secret stipends reached Pratapaditya he ordered Surma to go to her paternal home.

It expresses Basanta Ray’s lonely grief at being left behind in emptiness after those who were his, and whom he used to sing for, no longer answer his call, leaving him no joy in singing and asking how he can go on living with only himself. He first sings it alone on his veranda in Raigarh at sunset, his sitar absent, remembering his loved ones in Jessore and longing to embrace them. He sings it again in Jessore, taking Vibha’s hand after finding Surma’s room silent, dark, and empty and learning of Udayaditya’s imprisonment, as shared grief over the broken, deserted family.

Because she failed to stop the boat at the canal, Udayaditya escaped to Basanta Ray in Raigarh, and when Rukmini survived her jump into the canal, informed Pratapaditya that Udayaditya had escaped with the old king, and led his men to find Udayaditya in Raigarh, Pratapaditya ordered Muktiyar Khan to capture Udayaditya and execute Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra coldly and dismissively—refusing to send a welcome, light the path, or play the Nabat, greeting him without joy or haste with “Come. Are you well?” while attending to his minister and then sending him to the inner quarters—while in his own court Ramchandra approvingly presided over daily mockery that branded Pratapaditya’s family as kings for only two generations, of earthworm/leech origin, whose father begged Ramchandra’s grandfather for anointment with his left little toe, and claimed that Ramchandra’s marriage alone redeemed their seven generations and that bringing Pratapaditya’s daughter into his house would lower his honor.

The widow Rukmini left Raigarh, changed her name to Mangala, and settled on the outskirts of Jessore, where she befriended palace servants and learned palace news; when the Rajmahishi secretly sent Matangini to fetch medicine from her to win Udayaditya back from Surma, Mangala spent five days preparing a mantra-charged poison meant to kill Surma without arousing Udayaditya's pity, and Surma died after taking it.

He tells Pratapaditya, "I do not want your kingdom — grant me release from your throne," agrees that Samaraditya will be the heir, and that same day at the temple, in front of Pratapaditya, touches Ma-Kali's feet and swears that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of Jessore's kingdom, will not sit on its throne, and will not touch its royal scepter — if he ever does, the sin of his grand-uncle's murder will be his — then leaves for Kashi.

After Rammohan refused to take it to Jessore, Ramchandra gave the letter to old Nayanchand, who, fearing what Pratapaditya might do if it reached him, instead gave it to the Mahishi. She withheld it from Pratapaditya, mentioning only hypothetically that Ramchandra might one day abandon Vibha, and later showed the letter to Basanta Ray. On Basanta Ray's instruction, the Mahishi told Vibha and announced throughout the household that Ramchandra had written requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip, the opposite of the letter, which renounced Vibha and said she should not be sent again.
Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the large sal wood logs blocking the canal.

He leaves behind his eternal companion, the sitar, saying he will not play it anymore, after tears blurred his eyes and choked his throat and forced him to stop playing and put it down; later in Raigarh he says its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned, and he finds no joy in singing because those he used to sing for are no longer there.

Earlier he involved himself in the affairs of the subjects, went out whenever he pleased, acted against Pratapaditya's wishes, treated danger as a trifle, and would have stopped a royal official beating a subject without considering the consequences and fought oppression with all his might. After Surma's death his former courage is gone; he is extremely afraid of Pratapaditya, hesitates in every task, aborts going to intervene against the ordered looting and burning, runs into his house instead of stopping the beating, and no longer has the courage to help Bhagavat and Sitaram with money openly or secretly.
He pulls Udayaditya out of his prison cell during the fire and leads him away into the open field.

First, he carries Maharaj Ramchandra Ray on his back down a rope made from sheets tied to a pillar on the palace roof to his boat in the canal about seventy cubits below, gripping the rope in his teeth at its end to lower Ramchandra by hand into the boat before jumping down himself; second, after Vibha faints in the palace, he lifts her, carries her out, and places the unconscious Vibha in a palanquin at the gate.

In Jessore the Mahishi dresses Vibha with her own hands in eight thick gold bangles and one huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure the Mahishi restyles after Vibha has it redone to her own liking, leaving her shy, joyous, and utterly flustered. In Chandradwip she refuses a palanquin, saying she will go like a common subject and a beggar-woman, steps out dressed as a common woman, enters the palace like any other maidservant with her veil over her head, is not recognized or welcomed, and falls at the king's feet.

In his bedchamber, the window is where Surma used to sit. He sits there leaving her spot empty, and under the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, he hopes Surma will return, even imagining he hears her voice. The window thus symbolizes absence, grief, and waiting for the past.

In prison, the small window—showing a sliver of sky, bamboo grove, Shiva temple, and flying birds—is the one place where he feels free. Looking through it, he believes his cage and chains will one day break and he will be liberated; away from it, surrounded by darkness, he forgets that freedom. He therefore sits on the floor by the window instead of on the cot, which he calls his true prison, reversing the bedchamber symbolism.

Sitaram, a penniless palace guard attracted to Rukmini's beauty and silver, borrows from her repeatedly while flirting with her, calling her Subhadra, Pran, Priye, Priyatame, and Pranpriye, and joking about interest. Rukmini, who earns her living by lending money at interest and keeps many under her control by beauty and silver, feigns affection and gives him money she knows he is unlikely to repay. Sitaram forgets the debt, visits her frequently, and confers with her secretly about a scheme for which he says he will need Bhagavat's help.

When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram turns on her, cursing her and almost striking her, threatening to set her house on fire, grind her face on the stone floor, smear her face with lime and soot, and drive her from the city, while declaring he will free the Yubaraj. Rukmini replies that the Yubaraj is hers, that only she can do him good or harm, and that he will see how he manages to free him.

After Sitaram engineers the fire and fake death in the prison cell, he goes to Rukmini's cottage intending to steal her money, believing her dead. He finds her alive, wet, trembling, and ghost-like, having returned, as she says, from the door of Yama. She threatens to lay Sitaram and the Yubaraj in the oven and smear her body with ash from their pyres. Sitaram tries to feign affection to make up with her, but she becomes enraged, goes to search for a curved blade to make him pay, and repeatedly strikes the floor where he had stood. Realizing he is not ready to die from a real blade, he slips out, flees Jessore that night with his family for fear she knows about the escape, and Rukmini later exposes Sitaram's role to Pratapaditya.

Sitaram first used the fire in the row of guard huts near the prison as a distraction: five or six rooms caught fire simultaneously, the guards abandoned Udayaditya's door and ran to save their belongings, and Sitaram's men prolonged the chaos by pouring water where there was no fire, fetching water without bringing it back, breaking water pots, and stumbling into one another, so the fire would not go out despite the effort. While everyone was occupied and Udayaditya was taken out and away by boat, Sitaram's men set fire to the empty prison cell itself, burning its windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and wooden fences, and Sitaram threw bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the room. Reports then spread that the cell had caught fire, that the Yubaraj had been heard screaming inside, and that the roof had collapsed with no response, allowing Sitaram to spread the news that the Yubaraj had died in the fire and remain untroubled for some time.

He feels no gratitude for Udayaditya ignoring his own danger to save his life, believing it was bound to happen and that Udayaditya saved him only for the sake of his sister, not as his main objective, and he joins his courtiers in laughing at and ridiculing Udayaditya.

Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition in Yubaraj Udayaditya's name, sealed with the seal from Rukmini's ring, falsely stating that Udayaditya is lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi in order to get the kingdom for himself, and Bhagavat delivers it to Pratapaditya as a petition intercepted from Udayaditya's servant on his way to Delhi.

Vibha's hair marks Surma's presence because Vibha, finding the Mahishi's styling unbearable, secretly goes to Surma to have it done to her own liking — a style the Mahishi then undoes as Surma's jealous sabotage; after Surma is gone, Vibha sits at hair-braiding time waiting for Surma to come, the hair stays unbraided through evening and night, and Rammohan later finds it unkempt, signaling that no one is caring for her as Surma did.
